title: WHAT IF THE PERSON EVERYONE GAVE UP ON IS THE ONE GOD IS RESTORING?
paragraphs: WHAT IF THE PERSON EVERYONE GAVE UP ON IS THE ONE GOD IS RESTORING?
They remember who you were. They still whisper about what you did. They have already decided how your story ends. But what happens when Jesus walks into the very life everyone else has written off?
There is a kind of pain that doesn't come from being hated.
It comes from being remembered only for the worst thing you've ever done.
You can change your habits. You can walk away from the people who helped destroy you. You can spend nights crying before God, begging Him to make you someone different.
And still, somebody will bring up your past as though it happened yesterday.
They don't see the prayers.
They don't see the battles.
They don't see how many times you have reached for your old life and pulled your hand back because you remembered what Jesus rescued you from.
They only remember the scandal.
The addiction. The affair. The betrayal. The prison sentence. The divorce. The lies. The money you stole. The family you disappointed. The church you walked away from. The promises you broke.
And sometimes the most painful part isn't what other people say about you.
It's that somewhere deep inside, you have started believing them.
Maybe they're right.
Maybe I'll never change.
Maybe I've gone too far.
Maybe God is tired of hearing me apologize for the same things.
But before you decide that your worst chapter is your final chapter, I want you to walk with me into a story recorded in Scripture.
Because there was once a man so feared, so despised, and so associated with the suffering of God's people that when someone claimed Jesus had changed him, the believers were afraid to believe it.
His name was Saul.
And if you understand what Jesus did with that man, you may never look at a broken human being the same way again.
Saul wasn't merely misunderstood.
He was dangerous.
Acts 8:3 says he was ravaging the church, entering houses, dragging away men and women, and committing them to prison.
Imagine being a Christian mother in Jerusalem, hearing footsteps outside your door.
Imagine your children asking why you are frightened.
Imagine knowing that somewhere in the city was a man who believed destroying people like you was an act of religious faithfulness.
That was Saul.
He wasn't the kind of person Christians would have invited to lead a Bible study.
He was the kind of person they warned one another about.
And Scripture doesn't soften what he did to make his eventual transformation more comfortable.
In Acts 9:1, Saul was still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord.
The Greek text uses the expression ἐμπνέων ἀπειλῆς καὶ φόνου (empneōn apeilēs kai phonou), meaning "breathing threats and murder."
This was not a man who had simply made a few unfortunate choices.
His hostility had become part of the atmosphere of his life.
He was actively pursuing Christians.
And then came the road to Damascus.
Saul was traveling with authority to arrest followers of Jesus when a light from heaven suddenly shone around him.
He fell to the ground.
And a voice spoke.
"Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" (Acts 9:4, ESV)
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He didn't ask why Saul was persecuting an organization.
He didn't ask why Saul was attacking a religious movement.
Jesus said, "Why are you persecuting me?"
The people Saul had wounded belonged to Christ.
Their suffering mattered to Christ.
And the risen Lord identified Himself with those whom Saul had been terrorizing.
Then Saul asked the question that would change everything.
"Who are you, Lord?"
And Jesus answered:
"I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting." (Acts 9:5, ESV)
Imagine that moment.
The very Jesus Saul thought he was opposing for the sake of God was alive, exalted, and speaking directly to him.
Everything Saul had been certain about was collapsing.
His religious confidence.
His moral superiority.
His understanding of righteousness.
The identity he had built around being right.
All of it was being confronted by the One he had rejected.
And here is what should stop us in our tracks.
Jesus had every right to judge Saul.
Saul was guilty.
His victims were real.
His actions were evil.
Yet the Lord who confronted him also began the work of transforming him.
Not because Saul deserved a second chance.
Not because his crimes were insignificant.
But because the grace of Jesus Christ is greater than the righteousness sinners imagine they possess and more powerful than the sins that enslave them.
Saul rose from the ground unable to see.
The man who had traveled to Damascus believing he could see the truth more clearly than everyone else now had to be led by the hand.
For three days he was without sight, and he neither ate nor drank.
The Scripture doesn't tell us everything that passed through his mind during those three days.
We should not pretend to know.
But we do know that the man who entered that road breathing threats was no longer in control of his journey.
And somewhere else in Damascus, God was preparing another man for an assignment that would require extraordinary obedience.
His name was Ananias.
The Lord appeared to him in a vision and told him to go to Saul.
Ananias knew exactly who Saul was.
He had heard about the harm Saul had done to the saints in Jerusalem.
He knew Saul had authority to arrest those who called upon the name of Jesus.
So Ananias protested.
And can we be fair to him for a moment?
His fear wasn't imaginary.
Saul had actually hurt people.
The danger was real.
Sometimes Christians speak about forgiveness as though genuine wounds should simply disappear when someone says they have changed.
But Scripture never requires us to pretend that evil was harmless.
Forgiveness does not mean abuse never happened.
Grace does not erase the need for repentance.
Restoration does not automatically eliminate consequences, rebuild trust overnight, or require victims to place themselves back in danger.
God's mercy is not permission to ignore wisdom.
Yet listen to what the Lord said about Saul.
"Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel." (Acts 9:15, ESV)
A chosen instrument.
The persecutor.
The man believers feared.
The man whose name had been associated with suffering.
Jesus was declaring a purpose for his life that nobody watching his previous behavior would have predicted.
But there is something important here.
God did not call Saul a chosen instrument because persecution was somehow acceptable.
Christ was not celebrating Saul's former violence.
He was revealing what divine grace could accomplish in a sinner whom He had confronted and was transforming.
And then Ananias went.
He entered the house.
He laid his hands on Saul.
And the first words recorded from him in that encounter were extraordinary.
"Brother Saul." (Acts 9:17, ESV)
Brother.
Not monster.
Not enemy.
Not hopeless case.
Brother Saul.
Think about the weight of those two words.
Ananias wasn't denying Saul's past.
He was obeying the Lord who had revealed Saul's new direction.
The man who had once threatened the family of God was being received as a brother in Christ.
And if you have ever lived beneath the weight of your own reputation, you may understand why those words matter.
Because sometimes you can survive the consequences of your mistakes and still struggle to believe that you belong anywhere.
You walk into a room and wonder what people have heard.
You sit in church and wonder whether the person beside you would still shake your hand if they knew your history.
You hear a sermon about forgiveness and believe every word of it for everyone except yourself.
You know Jesus forgives sinners.
You just aren't sure He would welcome one like you.
But look at Saul.
The Lord did not merely stop his destructive path.
He brought him into the very community he had once attacked.
And that is where the story becomes even more uncomfortable.
Because the church still had to learn how to respond.
Acts 9:26 tells us that when Saul came to Jerusalem and attempted to join the disciples, they were afraid of him because they did not believe he was a disciple.
Can you imagine?
He had encountered the risen Christ.
He had begun proclaiming Jesus.
His life had taken a radically different direction.
But the believers remembered the old Saul.
And again, their fear was understandable.
A testimony does not instantly erase a history of violence.
Trust must be established through truth, wisdom, and observable fruit.
Then Barnabas stepped forward.
He brought Saul to the apostles and explained how Saul had seen the Lord, how Jesus had spoken to him, and how Saul had preached boldly in Damascus in the name of Jesus.
Barnabas did not invent a better past for Saul.
He testified to what Christ had actually done.
That distinction matters.
Christian restoration is not the art of making sinners look innocent.
It is the work of God bringing guilty people to repentance, forgiveness, and a transformed life through Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is why this story reaches so deeply into our own.
Because there are people who genuinely need to repent.
There are people who genuinely need protection from those who have harmed them.
And there are also people who have repented, turned from destructive ways, and begun walking with Christ, yet still find themselves permanently defined by what they used to be.
Sometimes the hardest thing for a community to believe is that God is doing something new in someone whose old life they remember too well.
But be careful.
The person you have reduced to a rumor may be someone Christ is teaching to pray.
The person you have dismissed as a failure may be someone Christ is bringing to repentance.
The person whose past you keep repeating may be someone Christ is patiently transforming.
And the person you think will never change may one day become a living testimony to the mercy of God.
That does not mean every claim of transformation is genuine.
It means we should neither be naïve about sin nor cynical about grace.
The Gospel gives us reasons to practice both discernment and hope.
Years later, Saul, also known as Paul, would describe himself with astonishing honesty.
In 1 Timothy 1:15, he wrote:
"Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost." (ESV)
The Greek phrase is ὧν πρῶτός εἰμι (hōn prōtos eimi), literally, "of whom I am first" or "foremost."
Paul wasn't claiming that Jesus had found an impressive man who needed a little improvement.
He was identifying himself as a sinner who had received extraordinary mercy.
And in the next verse, he explained why that mercy mattered.
He said he received mercy so that Jesus Christ might display His perfect patience as an example to those who would believe in Him for eternal life.
Read that again in your heart.
His story wasn't ultimately about Saul becoming famous.
It was about Jesus displaying His patience.
The testimony was not, "Look how strong I became."
It was, "Look how merciful Christ has been."
And that changes how we should tell our own stories.
Because the greatest evidence of restoration is not that everyone finally applauds us.
It is that Christ is being glorified through genuine repentance, persevering faith, growing obedience, and the fruit of a changed life.
Some people want restoration because they want their old reputation back.
But Jesus offers something greater than reputation management.
He offers reconciliation with God.
He offers forgiveness purchased through His blood.
He offers new life.
He offers the Holy Spirit, who works within believers to make them increasingly like Christ.
And none of this can be purchased through religious performance.
The Gospel is not a transaction where you become good enough to make Jesus accept you.
It is the good news that the sinless Son of God died for sinners and rose again, and that all who turn to Him in repentance and faith receive forgiveness and life in His name.
Paul himself would later write:
The Greek expression καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis) means "new creation."
Not merely a repaired public image.
Not a carefully managed appearance of holiness.
New creation.
The language points to the transforming reality of belonging to Christ.
It does not mean believers immediately become incapable of sin, never struggle again, or escape every earthly consequence of their past.
It means their identity and life are now fundamentally bound to the crucified and risen Savior.
And the God who begins His saving work does not abandon His people to transform themselves through willpower alone.
Perhaps you need to hear that tonight.
Because you've been trying to prove that you are no longer the person you were.
You've been exhausting yourself trying to convince people who have already decided not to believe you.
You've been replaying old conversations, imagining what you should have said, wondering how many years must pass before somebody stops introducing you through the lens of your failure.
But what if your deepest need isn't to win back every person's approval?
What if your deepest need is to keep surrendering yourself to the Lord Jesus Christ, whether the crowd recognizes His work in you or not?
What if the next step of obedience matters more than the next opportunity to defend yourself?
What if repentance is not merely saying, "I'm sorry," but turning toward Christ and allowing His truth to confront the very desires and patterns that led you into darkness?
And what if you stop treating the shame of your past as though it has greater authority than the cross of Jesus?
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction exposes sin and calls us toward repentance and Christ.
Condemnation tells us that our guilt is the final word.
But Romans 8:1 declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." (ESV)
That promise belongs to those who are in Christ.
It is not a blanket assurance that unrepentant sin is harmless.
It is a declaration that those united to Jesus are no longer under God's condemning judgment, because Christ has borne the judgment their sins deserved.
And perhaps this is where your heart begins to tremble.
Because you've spent years knowing what you've done.
But have you truly considered what Jesus has done?
The nails.
The cross.
The crown of thorns.
The darkness.
The innocent Savior giving Himself for the guilty.
The empty tomb announcing that death did not have the final word.
Your salvation does not rest on your ability to make your past disappear.
It rests on the finished work of Jesus Christ.
And if you are His, your past may explain where He found you, but it does not have the authority to define who you are in Him.
There is another story I want you to remember.
In Luke 15, Jesus told of a son who demanded his inheritance, left his father, and wasted his possessions in reckless living.
Eventually, he found himself hungry and humiliated, longing to eat what the pigs were eating.
Then he came to himself.
He decided to return home and confess his sin.
He did not return demanding recognition.
He did not come back insisting that his choices were misunderstood.
He came acknowledging that he had sinned against heaven and before his father.
And while he was still a long way off, his father saw him.
His father felt compassion.
His father ran.
His father embraced him.
His father kissed him.
And the son confessed.
The father then called for a robe, a ring, sandals, and a celebration.
But the older brother was angry.
He could not understand why the son who had wasted so much should be welcomed with such joy.
The father's response in Luke 15:32 reveals the heart of the parable:
"For this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found." (ESV)
The Greek word ἀπολωλώς (apolōlōs) means "lost," while εὑρέθη (heurethē) means "was found."
The language captures the movement from lostness to being found.
And in the context of Luke 15, Jesus was answering those who complained that He welcomed sinners.
This is not a story teaching that rebellion is insignificant.
The son really sinned.
His choices really brought ruin.
His confession mattered.
But the father's joy shows us something beautiful about the grace Jesus was revealing.
The return of a repentant sinner is not an inconvenience to be tolerated.
It is a reason for rejoicing.
Now ask yourself something uncomfortable.
When someone who has fallen begins turning back toward God, are you more like the father who rejoiced or the older brother who resented the celebration?
Do you secretly want some people to remain disqualified because you remember what they did?
Do you believe grace is powerful enough to save you but not powerful enough to transform someone who hurt you?
And if you are the one who wandered, have you mistaken the voice of shame for the voice of God?
The father in the parable did not call evil good.
He welcomed a son who had returned.
And Jesus told that story so we would understand the joy of heaven over sinners who repent.
Not the applause of people who have learned how to appear religious.
The joy of heaven over repentance.
That is the Gospel.
Not a celebration of scandal.
A celebration of grace that brings sinners home.
Maybe the person everyone gave up on is your son.
The one whose phone calls have become harder to answer.
The one who keeps promising he will change.
The one you love so deeply that every disappointment feels like another piece of your heart breaking.
You can love him without financing destructive choices.
You can pray for him without pretending that everything is fine.
You can maintain necessary boundaries while asking God to bring him to genuine repentance.
Or maybe it's your daughter.
The one who stopped attending church.
The one whose choices have become the subject of conversations you wish you never had to hear.
The one you still remember as a little girl falling asleep during family prayers.
Do not assume you can see everything God may be doing in her heart.
Keep speaking truth with love.
Keep praying.
Keep the door to honest conversation open where it is safe and wise.
Maybe it's your husband.
Maybe it's your wife.
Maybe it's your brother who returned from prison.
Maybe it's a former addict whose recovery has been painful and uneven.
Maybe it's someone whose name became a warning in your congregation.
And maybe, after all these words, you know exactly who this article is about.
You.
You are the person people stopped expecting anything from.
You are the one who has been trying to smile through the embarrassment.
You are the one who still hears the accusations long after everyone else has gone home.
You are the one who opens the Bible and wonders whether its promises could possibly include someone with your history.
Listen carefully.
I cannot promise that every relationship will be restored.
I cannot promise that every consequence will disappear.
I cannot promise that everyone who left will return.
And I will not tell you that every dream you once had is guaranteed to happen simply because you have started seeking God.
Scripture does not make those promises.
But I can tell you that Jesus Christ receives sinners who come to Him.
I can tell you that His mercy is not exhausted by the depth of human failure.
I can tell you that the same Lord who confronted Saul on the Damascus road is alive today.
And I can tell you that no sinner is beyond His power to save.
Jesus said in John 6:37:
"Whoever comes to me I will never cast out." (ESV)
Whoever.
That is not a small word.
It does not mean that repentance is optional or that we can follow Christ while deliberately embracing the sin He calls us to forsake.
It means that the sinner who truly comes to Jesus will not find a Savior unwilling to receive them.
You do not have to make yourself worthy of His grace before you come.
You come because you need His grace.
And His grace does not leave you comfortable in the darkness that was destroying you.
It teaches you to turn away from ungodliness and to live a new life before Him.
That is why the story of Saul matters.
He did not encounter Jesus and then return to persecuting Christians as though nothing had happened.
His direction changed.
His message changed.
His allegiance changed.
The man who once tried to silence the name of Jesus began proclaiming that Jesus is the Son of God.
And the transformation cost him dearly.
The former persecutor became a persecuted witness.
The man who once possessed authority to imprison believers eventually endured imprisonment himself for the sake of Christ.
He suffered.
He served.
He persevered.
Not perfectly.
Not independently of grace.
But as a man whose life had been claimed by the risen Lord.
And when he spoke about his accomplishments, he ultimately pointed away from himself.
"By the grace of God I am what I am." (1 Corinthians 15:10, ESV)
That is what restoration is supposed to produce.
Not arrogance.
Not spiritual celebrity.
Not a new way to glorify ourselves.
Gratitude.
Humility.
Obedience.
Love for Christ.
Compassion for sinners.
And a life increasingly shaped by the truth of God's Word.
So before you give up on someone, remember Saul.
Before you assume that somebody's past has permanently disqualified them from the mercy of God, remember the cross.
Before you decide that repentance is impossible for the person who hurt you, remember that salvation belongs to the Lord, not to our predictions.
And before you use somebody else's transformation as an excuse to ignore accountability, remember that the same grace that forgives also teaches us to live differently.
We need both truth and mercy.
We need courage to confront sin and humility to recognize that we ourselves survive only by the grace of God.
We need churches where wounded people are protected, repentance is taken seriously, and genuine transformation is neither dismissed nor manufactured.
We need believers who will not confuse suspicion with discernment or emotional excitement with spiritual maturity.
And we need to remember that Jesus is the Savior.
Not the church's reputation.
Not a charismatic testimony.
Not the approval of an audience.
Jesus.
There is a reason Gospel Warrior exists.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is sitting alone with a Bible they barely know how to read.
Someone is fighting the temptation to return to an addiction.
Someone is grieving a marriage that has fallen apart.
Someone is quietly wrestling with sin while everyone around them assumes they are spiritually strong.
Someone is one honest conversation away from admitting that they desperately need help.
And someone has been told so many times that they will never change that they have almost stopped asking God to change them.
We want the truth of Scripture to reach those people.
Not watered-down encouragement that tells them everything is fine.
Not condemnation that leaves them buried beneath shame.
But the Gospel of Jesus Christ, which exposes our sin, reveals our Savior, calls us to repentance, and announces the astonishing mercy of God.
That is why we keep writing.
Why we keep sharing Scripture.
Why we keep pointing people back to the cross.
Because a believer who has been rescued by grace needs more than a moment of inspiration.
We need to be rooted in the Word.
We need to learn how to pray.
We need to understand sound doctrine.
We need to grow in holiness.
We need to recognize false teaching.
We need encouragement when obedience is costly and correction when our hearts begin drifting.
And we need to remember, again and again, that the Christian life is not sustained by emotional excitement but by the faithful grace of God.
Not because financial support purchases God's favor.
And certainly not because anyone can buy forgiveness, blessing, or spiritual restoration.
Those things cannot be purchased.
But because Gospel-centered teaching, discipleship resources, and outreach require people willing to give, serve, and share.
Scripture says in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
"God loves a cheerful giver." (ESV)
And that same verse teaches us not to give reluctantly or under compulsion.
So please understand this clearly.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ and a life of grateful obedience.
But if you believe this ministry is bearing good fruit, supporting its work can be one practical way to participate in spreading biblical truth.
Those products are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
Not simply to increase its reach.
Someone who appears confident may secretly be drowning in guilt.
Someone who posts cheerful pictures may be terrified that God has given up on them.
Someone who has stopped attending church may still be wondering whether there is a way home.

And if one person is encouraged to open the Bible, confess sin, seek help, return to Christian fellowship, or call upon Jesus Christ because they encountered the Gospel through something you shared, that is worth caring about.
And if this message brings to mind someone whose struggles are private, consider sending it to them personally rather than exposing their situation in public.
Love does not need to embarrass someone in order to reach them.
I also want to ask you something, and I hope you will answer from the heart.
Have you ever been the person everyone thought would never change?
Or have you ever watched God transform someone you had nearly given up on?
You don't need to share details that would expose another person's private struggles.
You don't need to tell the world everything you've survived.
But your honest testimony may remind someone that they are not alone.
If you are weary and need the prayers of fellow believers, comment, "Pray for me."
Not as a formula.
Not as a way to earn a miracle.
But as an honest expression of your need for grace and Christian encouragement.
For the nights when you feel tempted to believe that your failures have greater power than the promises of Christ.
For the moments when somebody else's past makes it difficult for you to believe that restoration is possible.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, those who have drifted from the faith, and even those who are still searching for answers about Jesus.
Let them know there is a place where they can encounter the Word of God and be pointed toward the Savior who alone can give eternal life.
What if the person everyone gave up on is the one God is restoring?
What if you have been so focused on their yesterday that you have failed to notice the first genuine signs of repentance today?
What if you have been so ashamed of your own history that you have forgotten the Savior who died to redeem sinners?
What if the man you once knew as a persecutor is now the man Christ has called to preach?
What if the prodigal you thought would never return is already beginning to turn toward home?
What if the person who cannot yet imagine a future of obedience is sitting in the very place where God's Word is beginning to break through years of deception?
We do not know everything God will do in another person's life.
And we must never claim to know what Scripture has not revealed.
But we know what He has already done in Jesus Christ.
The cross is real.
The resurrection is real.
The call to repentance is real.
The offer of forgiveness is real.
And the power of God to make sinners new is real.
Perhaps you are reading this while carrying the weight of something you have never fully confessed.
You know the truth.
You know the excuses.
You know the promises you have made and broken.
You know the things you have hidden behind your smile.
And you are tired.
So tired.
Then don't settle for merely feeling emotional about this article.
Turn to Jesus.
Confess your sin to God.
Stop defending what He calls evil.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
Seek wise, biblical support and take the practical steps necessary to turn away from destructive behavior.
If you have harmed others, pursue appropriate accountability and restitution where possible, without demanding that those you wounded immediately trust you again.
And keep following Christ, even when the road is slow.
Because restoration is not always dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like telling the truth when lying would be easier.
Sometimes it looks like walking away from temptation when nobody is watching.
Sometimes it looks like accepting consequences without bitterness.
Sometimes it looks like asking forgiveness without expecting a particular response.
Sometimes it looks like returning to Scripture after months of silence.
Sometimes it looks like getting up after a painful failure, confessing sin, and continuing to seek the Lord rather than surrendering to despair.
And sometimes the most beautiful evidence of grace is not a crowded room applauding a spectacular testimony.
It is one ordinary person, alone with God, quietly choosing obedience again.
That person may never become famous.
They may never stand behind a pulpit.
Their story may never receive thousands of shares.
But heaven does not measure the worth of a redeemed life by its popularity.
And Jesus did not shed His blood merely to create impressive testimonies.
He came to seek and to save the lost.
So if you are the person everyone gave up on, hear the Gospel one more time.
Your sin is serious.
But Christ is a sufficient Savior.
Your past is real.
But His mercy is real.
Your repentance must be genuine.
But His invitation is not reserved for people with spotless histories.
Come to Him.
And if you are the person standing on the other side, watching someone begin to change, do not let bitterness turn you into someone who secretly resents the possibility of grace.
Be wise.
Be truthful.
Maintain boundaries where they are needed.
But leave room for God to do what only God can do.
After all, there was a day when Saul was known for dragging Christians from their homes.
And there came a day when he could write to the church about the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.
The difference was not the power of positive thinking.
It was not human applause.
It was not a carefully constructed personal comeback.
It was Jesus.
The same Jesus who died for sinners.
The same Jesus who rose from the grave.
The same Jesus who confronted Saul.
The same Jesus who is still worthy of our repentance, faith, worship, and obedience today.
And perhaps the most unforgettable part of this story is that Saul was never its greatest miracle worker.
Jesus was.
He always was.
He always will be.
The world may keep a record of the person you used to be, but it cannot overrule the mercy of the Savior who makes sinners new.
